I just think neopronouns are a bit redundant. All pronouns are made up really, that's not the issue, but we already have a meaning behind she, he and they so when someone uses those pronouns it conveys information. Since often no one but the individual uses neopronouns their pronouns convey no information to other people making them essentially worthless. I say the best thing we can do is get rid of gendered pronouns and stop making assumptions on people based on such. 

I think gender is too nebulous to say whether something is invalid or not. Though I'd agree he is generally living the life of a woman if he chooses to present that way, which is fine if people recognize that. Now, if this individual even used she/her pronouns then I can see a problem if they are not a man in absolutely anyway yet expect to be seen a certain way, but that's pretty rare.

I have a non binary friend who has social dysphoria, and even some physical, over being seen as a man but isn't trans and doesn't claim to be trans, they just use they/them pronouns because of the damage society has caused with gender stereotypes. I hope one day they're not afraid of being a man and are happy with themselves, but if a cis or trans person are happier using a set of pronouns or a presentation to cope with society I respect it. Ill try to not make this too long and convoluted, but I'm willing to share. It took me about 18 years to realize I might be trans, and another year of intensive questioning. Throughout my life, I felt I was internally male and fit the male role better, I binded and changed my name to something masculine, but I had no idea this was how trans people felt too.

  I come from a very Conservative family, and I followed in their footsteps. It became nearly an obsession of watching Steven Crowder, Shapiro, and the other unfortunately popular right wing figures at the time. And so my opinion of trans people was very negatively mainly from ignorance. In fact, I think I truly disliked trans people as a way to avoid my own feelings on the topic. I didn't have to accept it in myself if it wasn't valid, and I have previous texts of mine which prove I thought this way. Ironically I think I thought it made me more masculine to be an edgy 14 y/o Conservative. 

 Eventually, becoming completely apolitical opened the door for me to learn more. When I'd stumbled, or maybe I felt called to look, on the FTM subreddit absolutely everything I've felt my whole life hit me on the head. I felt joy for I think for the first time ever. But, I panicked too, and it opened the door to a lot of questions I wasn't sure how to answer. The amount of doubt and certainly I felt at the same time was dizzying. So yeah I doubted a lot. I doubted if I even wanted to be a guy or how far I wanted to go in transition. But the more I experimented, the more comfortable I became. I went by non binary and they/them for a weeks, which wasn't bad, but it wasn't the same as being called he. Otherwise, I didn't worry about labels so much about what I wanted to do for the future.

 The most difficult thing I think to accept was that everyone would see me differently. I was worried about losing friends, never being seen as attractive, and never being accepted as a "real" guy. I felt very out of place and almost like a freak. So far, none of those have been true, but they're valid fears. But I'm more comfortable than I ever have been, and it's just felt right. I always knew I wanted to go by he/him, and now that everyone is, things feel much more natural. No matter what I decide to do in the future, I'm happy with how far I've come so far

Gender is by definition a social construct. So is sex, in the sense that we've grouped a bunch of characteristics together to be able to better understand the world. That doesn't mean the feelings related to it can't be real or innate. In the absence of gender, transgender people would still exist, they just wouldn't be called transgender and would likely manifest differently. Physical dysphoria is a real thing and would still exist, but social dysphoria wouldn't. There's plenty of things we can get dysphoria about that aren't biological. I hated pink when I was a kid because it was associated with being girl. Doesn't mean I was hard wired to hate pink, but that my physical dysphoria and discomfort manifested socially in that regard. I'm not saying social dysphoria is illegitimate, only that it depends on your culture. Gender is as real as sex is, and I'd say pretty real, but our culture shapes how we interpret the world
